name: Korean gagok lyric-song
lineage: Korean gagok lyric-song tradition. Gagok is the formal courtly literary-chamber lyric-song genre of the Joseon-dynasty literati class (yangban), with origins traced to the late Goryeo through middle-Joseon periods (fifteenth-seventeenth centuries) and the canonical repertoire codified through the Cheong-gu-yeong-eon and Hae-dong-ga-yo song-book anthologies. Performance configuration: solo singer (male or female, with distinct namchang men's-repertoire and yeochang women's-repertoire repertoires) accompanied by the canonical jeongak ensemble — geomungo (six-string fretted board-zither, struck with bamboo plectrum), gayageum (twelve-string moveable-bridge plucked board-zither), daegeum (large bamboo end-blown flute), piri (cylindrical-bore double-reed pipe), haegeum (two-string upright fiddle), and janggu (hourglass barrel-drum). Twenty-six canonical men's songs and fifteen canonical women's songs constitute the core repertoire. Sijo poetic-form (three-line structure: initial verse, parallel verse, conclusion-with-twist) provides the lyric base. Slow tempo (a single song can take ten to fifteen minutes), wide melisma, and characteristic pitch-and-amplitude vibrato (nonghyeon) define the vocal aesthetic. Cho Soon-ja and Lee Dong-gyu among the twentieth-century canonical performers; the National Gugak Center maintains the institutional transmission. Distinguished from sijo (the closely-related but more austere sung-poetry form) by gagok's full ensemble accompaniment and longer melodic-elaboration register; distinguished from gasa (the longer narrative-lyric form) by gagok's strict sijo-poetic-meter base; distinguished from minyo folk-song by gagok's literary-chamber-with-jeongak-ensemble functional context.
